name: Voice & multimodal interfaces
summary: Talking to AI out loud and showing it images or video, through phones, cars, speakers and glasses.

D1.guide: Predict: why does a slow reply feel worse when speaking than typing?
text: You can talk to some AIs out loud, and they talk back.
You can also show them a photo, or point a camera at something, and ask what it is.
D1.analogy: A phone call that can switch to video when you need to show something.

text: The older design is a **pipeline**: speech-to-text turns your voice into words, a text model replies, and text-to-speech reads the reply aloud. Each step adds delay, and tone of voice is lost.
Newer **speech-to-speech** models take audio in and produce audio out directly, so they can reply faster, cope with interruptions and keep emphasis and emotion.

Images and video work in a similar way: a vision-capable model turns pictures into tokens alongside the text. Voice and cameras make AI usable hands-free, in cars, on glasses and for people who find typing hard.

diagram.caption: Two ways to build a voice assistant

columns.title: Pipeline
points: Easy to swap parts; slower; tone lost

D2.analogy: A phone call that can switch to video.
D2.analogyBreaks: A friend on video watches continuously and remembers what they saw. Many assistants look at a single photo or a few frames, and can confidently describe things that are not there.

predict.question: In a voice pipeline, which change most shortens the pause before the assistant starts speaking?
options: Streaming: speak the first words while the rest is still being generated
Asking people to talk more slowly
predict.explanation: Streaming lets each stage start before the previous one finishes, so the person hears a reply before the full answer exists.

text: Open problems: natural turn-taking and interruptions, the privacy of always-listening microphones and cameras, voice cloning used for fraud, and accents and languages that speech recognisers handle less well.
